articles.label: Government
articles.headline: Escambia County's Short-Term Rental Fight Heads to Court
articles.dek: Property owners sue over new licensing rules as county commissioners defend restrictions they say protect neighborhood character. The outcome could reshape rental policy across the Panhandle.
brief: A group of 14 property owners filed suit in Escambia County Circuit Court challenging the county's short-term rental ordinance enacted in March
The lawsuit argues the licensing caps and proximity requirements constitute an unconstitutional taking of property rights
Legal experts say the case could set precedent for how Florida counties regulate vacation rentals following the state's 2023 preemption rollback
articles.body:
The courtroom on the third floor of the M.C. Blanchard Judicial Building was empty Wednesday morning except for a clerk sorting files. In six weeks, it will be standing room only.

That's when Circuit Judge Jan Shackelford will hear oral arguments in Beachside Properties LLC v. Escambia County, a lawsuit that pits 14 property owners against the county government over who gets to decide what happens inside their homes when they're not there.

The stakes extend well beyond the plaintiffs' rental income. Attorneys on both sides acknowledge the case could establish precedent for how Florida's Gulf Coast counties regulate short-term rentals—a $4.2 billion industry in the Panhandle alone, according to Visit Florida data.

What the ordinance does

Escambia County commissioners voted 4-1 in March to impose the strictest short-term rental regulations in the county's history. The ordinance caps licenses at 8% of residential units per census tract, requires 1,000 feet of separation between new rentals, mandates 24-hour local property managers, and establishes a three-strike enforcement system that can revoke licenses permanently.

Existing rentals were grandfathered in—but only if owners applied for licenses within 90 days and passed inspection. County records show 847 properties qualified. Another 312 applications were denied or withdrawn.

Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, who sponsored the ordinance, called it a compromise between property rights and neighborhood preservation.

"We're not banning short-term rentals," Bergosh said at the March meeting. "We're managing them. That's what local government does."

Commissioner Doug Underhill cast the lone dissenting vote, arguing the restrictions would drive rental activity underground and reduce tax revenue.

The lawsuit's claims

Filed June 3, the complaint advances three constitutional arguments. First, that the density caps and proximity requirements constitute a regulatory taking under the Fifth Amendment by eliminating economically viable use of the properties. Second, that the ordinance violates equal protection by treating similarly situated property owners differently based on arbitrary geographic boundaries. Third, that the 90-day application window was insufficient notice and violated due process.

Lead plaintiff Beachside Properties LLC owns four single-family homes near Perdido Key. Three qualified for licenses. The fourth, purchased in February 2026, sits 940 feet from an existing licensed rental—60 feet short of the required separation.

"My client bought that property specifically for short-term rental use," said Thomas Eddins, the Pensacola attorney representing the plaintiffs. "The county changed the rules after closing. That's textbook regulatory taking."

The complaint seeks declaratory judgment that the ordinance is unconstitutional, an injunction blocking enforcement, and unspecified damages.

The county's defense

County Attorney Alison Rogers filed a motion to dismiss on July 15, arguing the plaintiffs lack standing because they suffered no concrete injury—their properties retain value for long-term rental or owner occupancy—and that the ordinance falls squarely within the county's police powers.

"Zoning has always involved winners and losers," Rogers wrote. "The Constitution does not guarantee property owners the most profitable use of their land."

Rogers also cited the Florida Legislature's 2023 decision to partially roll back state preemption of local short-term rental regulation. That law, which took effect July 1, 2024, explicitly authorized counties to impose registration requirements, density limits, and safety standards—the exact tools Escambia County deployed.

"The Legislature gave us this authority," Rogers said in an interview. "The plaintiffs' quarrel is with Tallahassee, not the Board of County Commissioners."

The legal landscape

Florida courts have not definitively ruled on how far local governments can go in restricting short-term rentals. The closest precedent is a 2019 First District Court of Appeal decision, Phantom of Clearwater v. Pinellas County, which upheld a registration requirement but explicitly declined to address density caps.

David Powell, a land use attorney in Tallahassee who is not involved in the Escambia case, said the outcome likely hinges on how Judge Shackelford interprets the 2023 preemption rollback.

"The Legislature opened a door, but it didn't say how wide," Powell said. "Escambia is testing the edges. If they win, you'll see similar ordinances in Bay County, Walton County, everywhere with beach tourism pressure."

Walton County, home to the 30A corridor, has already drafted but not adopted a density-cap ordinance. County officials there confirmed they are monitoring the Escambia litigation.

What neighbors say

On Perdido Key Drive last week, the conflict was visible in competing yard signs. "Save Our Neighborhoods" placards—distributed by a group called Perdido Residents United—stood three doors down from "Property Rights Matter" signs staked by the Escambia County Property Owners Coalition.

Barbara Kendrick has lived on the key for 22 years. The house next door became a short-term rental in 2019. She said the problems started immediately: late-night noise, overflowing trash, strangers parking across her driveway.

"I called code enforcement 14 times in two years," Kendrick said. "Nothing changed until the new rules. Now it's quieter. I actually know my neighbor again."

Two blocks east, Mark Salinas owns two rental properties that qualified for licenses. He opposes the density caps on principle but acknowledges the ordinance hasn't hurt his business.

"My bookings are up because there's less competition," Salinas said. "But that doesn't make it right. If they can do this to the guy down the street, they can do it to me next."

The money question

Escambia County collected $2.1 million in tourist development taxes from short-term rentals in fiscal year 2025, according to the Tax Collector's office. That revenue funds beach renourishment, tourism marketing, and debt service on the Pensacola Bay Center.

The ordinance included no fiscal impact analysis. County Administrator Wes Moreno said the administration expects minimal revenue effect because existing rentals were grandfathered and tourism demand remains strong.

"We're not trying to eliminate short-term rentals," Moreno said. "We're trying to manage growth in a way that protects quality of life for permanent residents."

The plaintiffs' complaint disputes that characterization, noting that 312 denied applications represent potential tax revenue the county chose to forgo.

What happens next

Judge Shackelford scheduled oral arguments on the motion to dismiss for September 12. If she denies the motion, the case proceeds to discovery and likely trial in early 2027. If she grants it, the plaintiffs will almost certainly appeal to the First District Court of Appeal.

Either way, the litigation will take months or years to resolve. In the meantime, the ordinance remains in effect.

Eddins, the plaintiffs' attorney, said his clients are prepared for a long fight.

"This isn't just about 14 property owners," he said. "It's about whether county commissioners can pick winners and losers in the real estate market. We think the Constitution says they can't."

Rogers, the county attorney, offered a different framing.

"This is about whether elected officials can respond to their constituents' concerns about their neighborhoods," she said. "We think the Constitution says they can."

The courtroom on the third floor will sort it out.

articles.label: Development & Infrastructure
articles.headline: The $40 Million Bet on West Cervantes
articles.dek: A Miami developer is buying up parcels along one of Pensacola's most blighted corridors. Longtime business owners aren't sure whether to sell or hold on.
brief: Miami-based Cordova Capital Partners has quietly acquired 23 parcels along West Cervantes Street since January, spending approximately $40 million on properties between A Street and Pace Boulevard
The firm's acquisition strategy has triggered a wave of unsolicited offers to remaining property owners, with some longtime business owners reporting purchase offers at three times assessed value
City officials confirm preliminary discussions about infrastructure improvements to the corridor but say no formal development agreements or tax incentive packages have been approved
articles.body:
The check engine light in Raymond Tate's 1994 Ford F-150 has been on for six years. He knows because he's been staring at it from behind the counter of Tate's Muffler & Brake on West Cervantes Street for just as long, watching traffic thin out and storefronts go dark up and down the block.

Two months ago, a man in a linen suit knocked on his shop door with an offer to buy the property for $1.2 million. Tate's father bought it in 1978 for $34,000.

"I told him I'd think about it," Tate said. "I'm still thinking."

He's not alone. Since January, a Miami-based investment firm called Cordova Capital Partners has quietly assembled 23 parcels along a mile-and-a-half stretch of West Cervantes, from A Street to Pace Boulevard. Property records reviewed by The Flightline show the acquisitions total approximately $40 million, making it the largest single real estate play in Pensacola's urban core in at least two decades.

The purchases have remained largely under the radar. Cordova used a network of LLCs with names like Emerald Gulf Holdings and Palafox Corridor Investments to acquire the properties, a common strategy that obscures ownership until deeds are recorded. Corporate filings traced by The Flightline link all the entities to the same registered agent in Miami.

Cordova Capital did not respond to multiple requests for comment over a three-week period.

The Corridor

West Cervantes Street is not pretty. Drive it on any given Tuesday afternoon and you'll pass check-cashing stores with barred windows, vacant lots where kudzu has swallowed the chain-link fencing, and buildings that haven't seen fresh paint since the first Bush administration. A 2019 city planning study labeled it "severely underutilized" and noted vacancy rates exceeding 40 percent in some blocks.

But the corridor has assets that spreadsheets love. It runs straight from Interstate 110 to the heart of downtown. It has four lanes. The land is cheap relative to its zoning—most parcels allow commercial or mixed-use development by right. And it sits just north of a neighborhood that has seen home values double since 2020.

"Someone was always going to do this," said Marcus Webb, a commercial real estate broker with Pensacola-based Sterling CRE who is not involved in the Cordova transactions. "The math has been staring at people for years. It just took someone with enough capital to move first."

Webb estimates that Cordova is paying, on average, 60 percent above assessed value for the parcels. That premium suggests the firm is betting on significant appreciation—or already has development plans that would justify the cost.

What's Coming

City records offer some clues. In April, Cordova's registered agent in Florida submitted a public records request seeking all available planning documents, traffic studies, and utility capacity assessments for West Cervantes between A Street and Pace. The request ran 11 pages.

Pensacola Mayor D.C. Reeves confirmed in an interview that city officials have met with representatives of Cordova twice this year.

"They've expressed interest in a significant mixed-use development," Reeves said. "Retail, multifamily housing, possibly some hospitality. But nothing has been submitted formally. No site plans. No incentive requests."

Reeves declined to characterize the city's posture toward the project beyond saying the administration is "open to conversations about responsible development."

Escambia County property records show that Cordova has not yet applied for any demolition permits, rezoning variances, or development approvals on its West Cervantes holdings. The parcels sit in a Community Redevelopment Area, which would make any future project eligible for tax increment financing—a tool that captures increased property tax revenue to fund infrastructure improvements benefiting the development.

CRA Executive Director Keisha Brown said no TIF applications are currently pending for the corridor.

The Holdouts

Cordova's buying spree has created a new class of property owners along West Cervantes: those who haven't sold yet.

Some didn't get offers. Others got them and declined. A handful are still weighing their options, caught between loyalty to a block they've worked for decades and numbers that would change their lives.

Linda Tran owns a nail salon in a strip center near Pace Boulevard. She's been there since 2003. Her landlord sold the building to a Cordova-linked LLC in February for $890,000. Tran said her new property manager called last month to inform her that her lease, which expires in October, would not be renewed.

"They told me I had ninety days," Tran said. "Twenty-three years and ninety days."

She's looking for a new location but said comparable spaces are running $2,000 a month more than she's paying now. She hasn't told her employees yet.

Other owners find themselves in the opposite position—suddenly holding leverage they never expected.

Robert and Diane Stokes own a half-acre lot with a small warehouse they've leased to a plumbing supply company since 1991. They received a written offer of $1.1 million in March. The Escambia County Property Appraiser's office assessed the parcel at $412,000 last year.

"We're retired," Robert Stokes said. "We don't need the money today. But our kids might need it tomorrow. So we're waiting to see what happens next door, and next door to that."

The waiting game is rational. If Cordova's development materializes and succeeds, remaining parcels become more valuable. If it stalls or fails, owners are left holding properties on a corridor that hasn't changed in 30 years.

History's Lessons

Pensacola has seen this story before, with mixed results.

In 2006, a Georgia-based firm assembled parcels along the bayfront with plans for a $200 million condominium and marina complex. The project collapsed during the financial crisis. Some of those properties sat vacant for a decade.

More recently, the redevelopment of the former Pensacola News Journal building into a mixed-use complex has been hailed as a model for urban infill. That project took seven years from initial acquisition to completion.

Webb, the broker, said the difference often comes down to the developer's staying power.

"The question isn't whether West Cervantes needs investment," he said. "It's whether this particular group can see it through. That takes capital, patience, and a city willing to partner."

Cordova Capital's portfolio, according to its website, includes apartment complexes in Tampa and Fort Lauderdale, a shopping center in suburban Atlanta, and a mixed-use development in Charlotte that broke ground in 2024. The firm does not disclose its assets under management.

What Tate's Thinking

Back at the muffler shop, Raymond Tate is watching a technician rotate tires on a Honda Civic. The air smells like burnt rubber and motor oil. The air conditioning unit in the window rattles loud enough to drown out the traffic outside.

Tate is 62. His father started the shop. His son has no interest in taking it over.

"The guy in the suit said they'd let me stay open through the end of the year if I signed," Tate said. "Said they'd even cover moving costs if I wanted to relocate."

He hasn't signed anything. He hasn't called them back. He's not sure what he's waiting for.

"I keep thinking about my dad," he said. "He bought this place because nobody else wanted it. It was a dump. He made it into something. And now somebody wants it because of what he did."

He paused.

"Maybe that's the answer. Maybe that's the whole point."

He went back to watching the Civic.
